passage: Admirers of vernacular building, the houses and barns put up by people who were not architects, often describe them as stores of climatic wisdom. The thick earth walls of a desert village keep rooms cool through the afternoon and release their stored warmth at night; the steep roofs of a snowy valley shed their load before it can crush the rafters; the raised floors of a flood plain let the water pass beneath. Each form, on this account, is the answer a community reached after centuries of trial, and modern builders, with their sealed glass boxes and mechanical cooling, would do well to copy it.

There is much truth in this, but the story is told too kindly. The forms that survive to be admired are the ones that worked well enough to be kept; the failures, the houses that collapsed and the villages abandoned after a bad decade, left nothing for us to photograph. What we see is therefore a filtered record, and it flatters the past. More important, vernacular forms were shaped by poverty and scarcity as much as by climate. People built with earth because earth lay underfoot and cost nothing to carry, not because they had compared it with every other material and found it best. A thick wall may be cool, but it may also be dark, damp in the rains and laborious to patch every year, and those who lived behind it bore those costs whether or not their admirers mention them.

None of this makes vernacular building less worth studying. It suggests, however, that the lesson lies in the method rather than in the forms. What village builders did well was to adjust slowly and continuously to the conditions in front of them, keeping what worked and changing what did not, with materials whose behaviour they knew intimately because they handled them every season. Their knowledge was local by necessity, and its strength was precisely that it never pretended to be anything else.

A modern builder who copies the outward shape of a courtyard house in a different climate, with different materials and a different way of living, has learned nothing from it, however picturesque the result. One who studies local sun, wind and rain with the same patience, builds, watches what happens and is willing to revise, has learned a great deal, even if the building that results looks nothing like a village house.

passage: In a number of countries a newborn cannot simply be given whatever name the parents choose. A registrar may refuse a name that is judged offensive, that does not clearly indicate whether the bearer is male or female, that is spelt in a way the national orthography does not allow, or that does not appear on an official list. Defenders of such rules usually present them as a modest form of child protection. Parents, the argument runs, are fallible and sometimes vain; the child carries the name for a lifetime and had no say in choosing it; and the state, which already requires that children be schooled and vaccinated, may reasonably insist that they not be saddled with a label that will invite mockery.

There is something to this. A name is not a private ornament but a tool that other people use, and a name that cannot be pronounced, written on a form or read out in a classroom without laughter does impose a cost on the person who bears it. Cases in which parents have tried to register a brand name, a string of numbers or an insult are real enough, and few people would object to a registrar declining them. If the rules went no further than this, they would hardly be worth arguing about.

But they usually go much further, and the further they go, the less work the child-protection argument does. A rule that a name must indicate the bearer's sex protects no child from ridicule; it protects a social expectation. A rule that a name may use only the letters of the national alphabet does not shield the daughter of immigrant parents from mockery; if anything, it obliges her to carry an altered spelling of her grandmother's name, one that marks her at every roll call as someone whose family had to be corrected. An approved list, finally, protects children chiefly from novelty, and novelty is not a harm. Many names now regarded as solid and traditional were once eccentric inventions, and a register that had frozen the stock of names a century ago would have prevented most of them.

What the stricter rules actually defend, then, is the stock of names itself, treated as a piece of national heritage that private choices might erode. That is a coherent aim, and some will think it a worthy one. It should, however, be argued for openly as cultural policy and weighed against the interest parents have in naming their children as their own traditions require, rather than smuggled in under the language of protecting the young. A state that wishes to guard children from cruel names needs a short list of what is forbidden, not a long list of what is allowed.

passage: Moral relativism is often defended as the natural philosophy of a tolerant person. If moral claims are true only relative to the standards of a culture, the argument runs, then no culture is in a position to condemn the practices of another, and the proper attitude towards difference is one of respectful non-interference. The appeal of this reasoning is easy to understand, since much historical cruelty was committed by people who were certain that their own customs embodied universal truth and that this certainty licensed them to remake others by force.

Yet the argument has a curious structure. Its conclusion, that we ought to tolerate other cultures, is itself a moral claim, and it is plainly meant to hold universally: the relativist does not think tolerance is required only of cultures that happen to value it. A culture whose standards prized conquest would, by relativist lights, be acting rightly when it conquered. If relativism is true, the most a tolerant culture can say to such a culture is that tolerance is valued here, which is a report about itself rather than a reason addressed to anyone else. The relativist who wants tolerance to bind everyone has quietly helped himself to a non-relative principle.

None of this shows that relativism is false, and the defender has a reply. Perhaps the claim is not that relativism entails tolerance but that believing it tends to produce tolerant people, by weakening the confidence that fuels crusades. That may be true as a matter of psychology, though the historical record is mixed; doubt can make people gentle, but it can also leave them unable to object to anything at all. More importantly, the reply changes the subject. It defends relativism as a useful belief rather than a true one, and it concedes that the case for tolerance must be made on other grounds.

Those other grounds are not hard to find. One can hold that some moral claims are true for everyone and still think that humility about one's own judgements, respect for people's capacity to govern their own lives, and the dismal record of forced conversion all count strongly against intervention in most cases. Such a view is less comfortable than relativism, because it obliges one to say that some practices are wrong even while declining to stamp them out. But it has the advantage of being able to explain why tolerance matters, which relativism, for all its tolerant intentions, cannot.

passage: Thought experiments occupy an awkward place in the theory of knowledge. Scientists and philosophers have long used them to settle questions, and some of the most admired episodes in the history of physics turn on an imagined scenario rather than an actual measurement. Yet a thought experiment, by definition, collects no new data. The experimenter sits still and imagines. If we learn something about the world this way, it is not obvious where the information comes from, and two answers have dominated discussion.

According to the first, a thought experiment is an argument in disguise. Its vivid scenario can always be rewritten as a set of premises and a conclusion, and whatever it teaches, it teaches because the premises were already believed and the conclusion follows from them. The imagery is persuasive packaging, useful perhaps for teaching, but adding nothing to the logical content. According to the second, the best thought experiments give us something no argument could: a kind of direct intellectual insight into the necessary structure of nature, as if the mind could see a law of physics in the way the eye sees a colour.

Neither answer fits the most celebrated example well. Galileo asked his readers to imagine a heavy body and a light one tied together and dropped. If heavier bodies fall faster, as the received physics of his day held, the light body should hold back the heavy one, so that the pair falls more slowly than the heavy body alone; but the pair is heavier than the heavy body, so it should fall faster. The supposition contradicts itself, and the natural way out is that all bodies fall at the same rate, at least in the absence of a resisting medium. The argument reading can reconstruct this, but only by writing in premises that no one had formulated before the scenario was imagined: for instance, that the speed of a composite body must lie somewhere between the speeds of its parts. The insight reading, for its part, makes the result mysterious, as though Galileo had glimpsed a law rather than noticed a contradiction in what he and his readers already believed.

A better account is that thought experiments work by drawing on knowledge we have but have never made explicit. Everyone who has carried a load or watched things fall has a large stock of tacit expectations about how bodies behave. A well-constructed scenario brings these expectations to bear on a case where they collide with an explicit theory, and so exposes a tension that was there all along. What is new is not the information but its arrangement. This explains why thought experiments can be genuinely informative without new data, and also why they cannot be reduced to an argument that someone might have written down beforehand: the premises are found by running the scenario, not before it.

It also explains when they should not be trusted. Our tacit expectations were formed in a narrow band of experience, among objects of moderate size moving at moderate speeds. A thought experiment that asks us to imagine the very small, the very fast or the very distant invites us to apply those expectations where they were never tested, and the resulting conviction, however vivid, carries only the authority of the experience behind it. The method is neither a trick of rhetoric nor a window onto necessity. It is a way of interrogating what we already know, and it is exactly as reliable as that knowledge.

passage: Few ideas about teaching have travelled as far, or met as little resistance, as the notion that each learner has a style. Some children, it is said, are visual learners, others auditory, others kinaesthetic, and each will learn best when lessons are delivered in the matching form. The idea is attractive for honest reasons: it seems to respect individual difference, it gives teachers something concrete to do with that respect, and it fits the everyday experience that people do prefer some ways of taking in information to others.

The trouble lies in the step from preference to performance. That people report preferences is not in dispute. What the theory needs is something stronger: that a learner labelled visual will learn more from a visual lesson than from a spoken one, while a learner labelled auditory will show the reverse. Testing this requires sorting learners by style, teaching each group in both ways, and checking whether the advantage flips from one group to the other. When the claim has been tested in this demanding way, the predicted crossover has generally failed to appear. Learners tend, on the whole, to benefit from the same methods whatever label they carry, and whatever preference they would have reported if asked.

What does seem to matter is the fit between the form of a lesson and the content being taught. A coastline is better learned from a map than from a description, whoever the learner is; the sound of a language is better learned by listening; a knot is learned by tying it. Here the mode is chosen for the material, not for the student. The same holds in reverse: a pupil who insists that she learns best by listening will not master the shape of a coastline sooner because it is described to her aloud, however vivid the description. A teacher who presents geography through maps is not catering to visual learners, but simply using the form in which geographical knowledge is most naturally held.

None of this means that variety in the classroom is pointless. Moving between pictures, speech and activity can hold attention and can give a learner several routes back to the same idea. The objection is to the diagnosis rather than to the variety. Labelling a child as one kind of learner invites both the child and the teacher to treat the other channels as closed, and a child told that she is 'not a reading person' may come to believe it. The cost of the theory is not that it wastes a few lessons, but that it narrows expectations while appearing to widen them.

passage: It is often said that forgiveness must be earned. On this view, the wrongdoer must first acknowledge what he did, express remorse and, where possible, make amends; only then is the victim in a position to forgive, and to forgive earlier would be to excuse the wrong or to collude in pretending that it did not matter. The view has an attractive moral seriousness. It refuses to let forgiveness become a soft word for forgetting, and it insists that wrongs make demands on the people who commit them.

But the view also has an awkward consequence, for it puts the victim's moral recovery in the hands of the person who harmed her. A woman wronged by a former friend who has since died, or who simply refuses to admit anything, would on this account be permanently barred from forgiving. She could stop thinking about the wrong, or decide that it no longer troubled her, but she could not forgive, because the conditions for forgiveness depend on someone else's change of heart. It is strange to make one of the most personal acts a person can perform conditional on the cooperation of the one person least likely to give it.

A better account distinguishes between what forgiveness is and what makes it fitting. To forgive is to give up resentment and the claim to repayment while continuing to judge that the act was wrong. Understood in this way, forgiveness does not excuse anything, since the judgement of wrong remains in place. What an apology does is make forgiveness easier and, often, more appropriate, because it removes the reason that resentment had for persisting: the wrongdoer who sincerely apologises has, in effect, joined the victim in condemning what he did. Without an apology, forgiveness remains possible, but it is a gift rather than a response, and it is offered for the victim's reasons rather than the wrongdoer's.

This is not to say that unconditional forgiveness is always admirable. Someone who forgives every injury at once, before she has even registered that she was wronged, may be showing not generosity but a lack of self-respect, and forgiveness that comes too easily can signal that the forgiver does not believe she was owed anything. A person who is slighted again and again by the same colleague, and who forgives each slight as though nothing had happened, may also be teaching the colleague that such slights cost him nothing, which serves neither of them. The point is only that apology is one route to forgiveness rather than its gatekeeper.

passage: Along many mountain roads there are small paved areas where drivers are invited to stop, and a sign, often bearing the symbol of a camera, announces that a view is available. People get out, look, photograph and drive on. The arrangement seems so natural that its assumptions pass almost unnoticed: that the beauty of a landscape is something seen, that it is best seen from a particular spot, and that the right relation between a person and the land is that of a spectator standing before a picture.

These assumptions have a history. The habit of judging terrain by whether it composes well, with a foreground, a middle distance and a far horizon arranged as a painter might arrange them, was cultivated by travellers who had learned to look at scenery through the conventions of landscape painting, and some of them carried tinted mirrors or framing devices so that the real view would more closely resemble a canvas. We no longer carry such devices, but the camera and the viewpoint sign perform much the same function: they select, frame and fix. A landscape that cannot be composed into a pleasing rectangle tends, under this regime, to count as no landscape at all.

The costs are not merely aesthetic. Places that photograph poorly, a marsh, a stretch of flat scrub, a slow brown river, are more easily dismissed as empty and therefore more easily drained, cleared or built upon, even when they are richer in life than the dramatic gorge that everyone stops to admire. The spectator's posture, moreover, shrinks what nature has to offer. The smell of wet earth, the sound of insects, the feel of a slope underfoot and the slow change of light over an afternoon cannot be gathered from a lay-by in the two minutes before the engine is restarted, and a beauty that is only looked at from a fixed point is a beauty with most of its dimensions removed.

It would be ungrateful to dismiss the viewpoint altogether. For many people a framed view is where an interest in landscape begins; the sign that says 'look here' has taught countless travellers to look at all, and a habit of attention begun at a lay-by can grow into something larger. The trouble lies not in framing as such but in treating the frame as the measure of value. An appreciation of nature adequate to its object would have to include the unspectacular and the unframeable, and it would have to be practised on foot and over time, with the whole body rather than with the eye alone.

passage: Experts who manage risk often speak of the public with weary patience. People, they observe, fear the wrong things. They worry about a nuclear plant that has never harmed anyone in the district while driving, without a second thought, along a road that kills several of their neighbours every year. They demand inquiries after a single dramatic accident and shrug at the steady toll of falls in the home. On this account the task of policy is to correct a problem of perception: to replace vivid fears with sober numbers, so that resources follow expected deaths rather than headlines.

There is something to this, but less than its confidence suggests. When people are asked to describe what makes a hazard frightening, their answers are not random. Risks feel worse when they are imposed rather than chosen, when they could kill many people at once rather than a few at a time, when their effects are delayed or invisible, and when those who create them are not those who bear them. None of these features is captured by a count of expected fatalities, yet none of them is obviously foolish. A person who accepts the dangers of rock climbing but objects to a factory releasing an untested chemical into the river is not confused about arithmetic. She is drawing a distinction between a risk she has consented to and one that has been placed on her by others, and that distinction is a moral one that most legal systems also recognise.

Seen this way, the gap between expert and lay rankings of hazards is partly a disagreement about what the question is. The expert asks how many people will die; the citizen asks, in addition, whether the arrangement that produces those deaths is fair, controllable and worthy of trust. To call the second question irrational is to settle a dispute about values by redescribing it as a dispute about facts.

None of this makes dread a reliable guide. The features that make a hazard feel threatening can be manufactured by vivid reporting, and fear can drive choices that increase the very danger it is meant to avoid. If travellers abandon aircraft for cars after a well-publicised crash, they may exchange a small risk for a larger one without noticing the trade. The sensible response is neither to dismiss public fear as noise nor to treat it as a verdict. It is to take it apart: to ask which of its components reflect values that deserve a hearing in policy, and which reflect only the salience of a recent and alarming image.

passage: We tend to picture hospitality as the purest form of generosity: a door opened to someone who has no claim on us and nothing to give in return. The picture is not false, but it omits half of what the practice involves. In the many traditions in which welcoming strangers is held to be a sacred duty, the welcome is also a careful exercise of authority. The host decides where the guest will sit, what he will eat, when he will speak and, eventually, when he will leave. To accept hospitality is to accept, for a time, a place inside someone else's order.

This asymmetry is not incidental. A stranger arriving at a settlement is, from the settlement's point of view, an unknown quantity: he may be a trader, a refugee, a spy or a raider. Hospitality converts this uncertain figure into a guest, someone whose position is defined and whose conduct is now governed by rules that the host administers. The rituals that so often accompany a welcome, such as the offering of water, the sharing of salt or bread and the formal exchange of names, can be read as stages in this conversion. The guest who eats at the host's table has implicitly agreed not to harm the household, and the host, in turn, has made himself responsible for the guest's safety against third parties.

It is significant, too, that hospitality is so often limited in time. Many customs specify that a guest may stay a few days before his status must change; after that he becomes a dependant who works, a kinsman by adoption, or simply an unwelcome burden. The welcome is generous precisely because it is temporary. A guest who could stay forever on a guest's terms would gradually unsettle the household's order, and the host would cease to be master of his own house.

Some philosophers have pressed for an ideal of unconditional hospitality, a welcome that asks no questions and sets no limits. As a corrective to the suspicion with which outsiders are often treated, the ideal has force. But taken literally it would dissolve the very relation it seeks to purify. Hospitality requires a host, someone who is at home and who can therefore offer a place; if every condition is removed, there is no longer anyone in a position to welcome. The authority that makes us uneasy is not a corruption of hospitality. It is the condition that allows a stranger to be received at all.

passage: It is tempting to treat discarded scientific theories as simple errors, interesting only as warnings. The caloric theory, which held that heat is a subtle, weightless fluid flowing from hotter bodies into colder ones, is a favourite example. We now understand heat in terms of the disordered motion of the particles that make up matter, and nothing like a heat fluid exists. Yet to file caloric under mistakes is to miss what made it, for several decades, the most useful account of heat available, and to misunderstand how the theory that replaced it came to be built.

The fluid picture explained a great deal, and explained it naturally. It said why heat moves from hot to cold, as water runs downhill, and why a hot body and a cold one placed together settle at a common temperature. It made heat something that could be counted, conserved and tracked through a process, which encouraged careful measurements of how much heat different substances absorbed as they warmed or melted. Some of the most enduring results of early thermal science were first obtained by investigators who believed in caloric, and an influential analysis of steam engines, which showed that the work an engine can extract depends on the temperatures between which it operates, was framed entirely in its terms. That result survived the theory's collapse.

The difficulties were real, and they were noticed early. Observations of cannon being bored suggested that friction could produce heat, apparently without limit, for as long as the boring continued. If heat were a conserved fluid squeezed out of the metal, the supply should eventually have run out. Defenders of caloric had replies, some ingenious and some strained, and the theory survived the objection for decades. It is easy to call this stubbornness. It is more accurate to say that a theory which organises a large body of successful work is not abandoned because of one anomaly, particularly when no rival yet explains everything the old theory explained.

None of this is to say that false theories are as good as true ones, or that caloric deserved to last forever. It did, in the end, mislead: it could make no sense of heat turning into work and work into heat, which became central once engines were studied closely. The claim is narrower. A theory can be wrong about what something is while being right about many of the ways it behaves, and those behavioural truths can pass, nearly intact, to its successor. Judging past science only by whether its picture of reality was correct makes its history look like a series of failures, when much of it was a series of partial successes handed on.

passage: Few critical preferences are as widely shared as the preference for round characters over flat ones. A round character, in the usual formulation, has an inner life complex enough that it can change, contradict itself and still remain recognisable; a flat character is built around a single trait and can be summed up in a sentence. The first is praised as lifelike, the second tolerated as a convenience, useful for filling a drawing room or delivering a message but not to be mistaken for the real achievement of fiction.

Yet the preference rests on an assumption that deserves scrutiny: that the novel's central business is the representation of individual inner life. That has been the business of one powerful tradition, but it is not the only thing novels do. Many of the novels readers return to are as much about a society as about a self, and a society is felt in fiction partly through the people who never change: the aunt who has said the same thing at every family dinner for thirty years, the official for whom every request is a breach of procedure. Their fixity is not a failure of imagination. It is how the novel registers the pressure of a world that does not bend, against which its few changing figures can be measured.

Flat characters also carry much of fiction's comedy, which depends on repetition. A man who responds to every misfortune by consulting the same almanac is funny the third time precisely because he could not have done otherwise. Deepen him, give him a moment of doubt about the almanac, and the joke dissolves into pathos; this may be a gain, but it is a different book. There is, too, a case that flatness is closer to ordinary experience than critics allow. Most of the people we know, we know only by a few habits and phrases, and a novel that rendered every acquaintance in the round would misrepresent how other people actually appear to us, however much it flattered our sense of their depth.

This is not to invert the hierarchy. A novel peopled entirely by flat characters would be a cartoon, and the moment when a figure we had thought simple reveals unexpected depth remains one of fiction's great effects, though it depends on our having first taken him as simple. The point is that flat and round are not grades of achievement but different tools, suited to different tasks, and a criticism that rewards only one of them will misread every novel in which both are at work.

passage: Imagine a middle-income country that discovers large reserves of natural gas off its coast. Export earnings surge, foreign currency pours in, and the national currency rises in value. For a while the effects look wholly benign: imports become cheaper, the government collects more revenue, and wages climb as the gas sector and the services that cater to it compete for workers. Yet a decade later the country's manufacturers, who sell abroad against foreign rivals, may find themselves in serious trouble. A stronger currency makes their goods dearer in foreign markets, and the higher wages set by the booming sectors raise their costs at home. Factories close or move away, and the economy comes to rest ever more heavily on a single commodity. The pattern is common enough to have a name, Dutch disease, taken from the experience of the Netherlands after its large gas discoveries.

Some economists see nothing pathological in this. A country that finds itself rich in gas, they argue, should export gas and import the manufactures it once made, just as a country with fertile land should grow food. The movement of labour and capital out of factories is, on this account, the market reallocating resources to where they now earn most. To call it a disease is to mistake adjustment for illness.

The argument is coherent, but it assumes that the sectors lost can be regained whenever conditions change, and that assumption is doubtful. Manufacturing is not merely one way among others of earning foreign exchange. It is a place where workers acquire skills, where firms learn by doing, and where suppliers, engineers and managers accumulate knowledge that exists in no manual. Such capabilities take years to build and decay quickly once the firms that hold them have gone. Gas, meanwhile, is finite, and its price is notoriously volatile. When the price falls or the fields run down, the currency weakens and exporting becomes profitable again in principle, but the firms, skills and networks that would have taken advantage of the change no longer exist. The country finds that it cannot simply return to where it was.

The remedy, then, is not to leave the gas in the ground but to manage the boom so that it does not hollow out everything else. A government can save a large share of the windfall abroad, in a fund invested in foreign assets, which slows the rise of the currency and spreads the benefit across generations; it can spend at home at a pace the economy can absorb without bidding up wages across the board. Such measures are politically hard, because they ask citizens to forgo spending money they can see. But the alternative is to treat a temporary gift as permanent income, and to discover too late that the industries it displaced were not as replaceable as the theory assumed.

passage: In many large cities, a good part of the open space created in recent decades does not belong to the public at all. Developers are permitted to build taller or larger than the rules would otherwise allow on condition that they provide a plaza, an arcade or a garden that anyone may enter. The arrangement looks like an elegant bargain: the city gains open space without paying for it, and the developer gains floor area worth far more than the ground surrendered. Critics have long complained that the resulting spaces are often bleak, hidden or quietly discouraging, with benches too narrow to sit on and guards who appear the moment anyone lingers.

The usual form of the complaint is that these spaces are private, and that private space can never be truly public. This puts the matter in the wrong place. Ownership, by itself, settles very little. Many publicly owned squares are fenced at night, patrolled against skateboarders and stripped of seating to deter people who might sleep there, while some privately owned courtyards are generous, well kept and genuinely welcoming. If the test of publicness were the name on the title deed, we would have to call the first kind more public than the second, which is absurd.

What makes a space public is better described as a set of permissions: the right to be there without a reason, to stay without buying anything, to gather with others, to hand out a leaflet or to hold a placard. These permissions are exactly what private management is tempted to withdraw, not out of malice but because each of them is a small risk to the owner and none of them earns anything. A plaza can be open to all in the formal sense while being governed by rules, often unpublished, that make it public only for the well dressed and the briefly passing. The question to ask is therefore not who owns a space but who writes its rules, and to whom the writers must answer.

Seen this way, the bargain need not be abandoned; it needs to be completed. A city that trades floor area for open space is entitled to specify not only the dimensions of the plaza but the permissions that come with it, to publish them at the entrance, and to enforce them against owners as firmly as it enforces its building codes. Where it fails to do so, it has not acquired public space at all. It has paid, in floor area, for something that looks like a square and behaves like a lobby.

passage: Among serious readers there is a settled suspicion of the happy ending. A novel that closes with a wedding, a reconciliation or a recovered fortune is assumed to have flinched at the last moment, to have given its audience what it wanted rather than what its story required. An ending in death, separation or failure, by contrast, is credited with courage. The assumption behind the contrast is rarely stated but easy to reconstruct: life does not resolve itself neatly, so a book that resolves neatly must be telling a comforting lie. The suspicion is old enough to have become a reflex, and few readers who share it could say where they acquired it.

There is something to this, since the history of popular fiction is crowded with endings that arrive from outside the story, the unexpected legacy, the villain who repents in a paragraph, the rival who conveniently dies, and readers are right to feel cheated by them. Such endings resemble a rescue by a passing stranger: welcome, perhaps, but unconnected with anything the characters have done. But the fault in such endings is not their happiness. It is that nothing in the preceding chapters made them necessary. A catastrophe imposed in the same way, a heroine killed by a runaway carriage because the author wanted the book to feel weighty, is no less arbitrary and, being arbitrary, no more truthful.

The prejudice persists, I think, because it confuses two things that endings do. Every ending closes; it marks the point after which the story will not be told. Some endings also console; they leave the reader reassured about the world the book has shown. Closure is a formal necessity, since a story must stop somewhere, while consolation is a choice. The suspicious reader notices that happy endings console, objects to the consolation, and then mistakes the objection for an argument against closure itself, as though the honest book would be the one that refused to finish. Yet an unhappy ending closes just as firmly; it simply closes on a different note, and that note can be just as comfortably familiar to readers who have learned to expect gloom from serious fiction.

The better test, then, is an internal one: an ending is honest when it is the place towards which the book's own pressures have been carrying it, so that a reader looking back can see how the earlier pages prepared it, whether that place is a marriage or a grave. By this test some happy endings are among the hardest-won things in fiction, and some tragic ones are merely fashionable. The question to ask of an ending is not whether it pleases but whether it follows.

passage: For about a century after industrialisation, the working week in the richer economies shrank steadily, from something like sixty hours or more to around forty. Many observers assumed the trend would continue. If each generation could produce more in an hour than the last, it seemed natural that part of the gain would be taken as leisure, and confident predictions were made in the early twentieth century that the grandchildren of that era might work perhaps fifteen hours a week. In much of the rich world the decline instead slowed sharply after the middle of the century, and for many full-time professionals it appears to have reversed. The puzzle is not that people work at all, but that productivity kept rising while the hours of so many stopped falling.

The simplest explanation is that people chose income over time. Higher pay makes an hour of leisure more expensive, since each hour off now forgoes more, and it also makes people richer, so that they can afford more leisure. Which of these pulls is stronger is an empirical matter, and for a long period the second seemed to win. Perhaps, the argument runs, it simply stopped winning: people discovered new things to want faster than their incomes satisfied the old wants. A related account adds that much of what people buy matters to them chiefly in relation to what others have, so that a general rise in income buys no one a better position and the race to earn resumes at a higher level.

Both accounts treat hours as something workers choose, as they might choose how much bread to buy. That premise deserves more scrutiny than it usually receives. For most employees hours come attached to a job, and the menu of jobs is set largely by employers. A firm that pays a fixed cost for each person it hires, in recruitment, training, benefits and supervision, has good reason to prefer fewer people working longer to more people working less. In many professions, moreover, long hours have become a signal of commitment, and promotion goes to those who send it; a lawyer who would gladly trade a fifth of her salary for a fifth of her week may find that the trade is not on offer at all, or that it costs her far more than a fifth of her career. Under such conditions the hours we observe tell us what jobs offer, not what workers want.

The institutional account has a limitation of its own. It cannot easily explain why some people, given a genuine choice, still work very long hours, and it would be a mistake to deny that for many of them the work itself is the attraction. Nor are the averages uniform. In some economies the same decades that lengthened the week for well-paid professionals left many lower-paid workers with fewer hours than they wanted, pieced together from part-time or irregular shifts. An average that holds steady can conceal one group working too much and another too little.

What follows is that the old prediction failed less because of a mistake about human desire than because of a mistake about how labour markets work. The forecasters assumed that rising productivity would be divided between income and leisure by the free choices of workers. The division has in fact been made largely by the structure of jobs, and that structure can be altered: by rules on hours, by the way benefits are financed, by what firms choose to reward. Whether people would then work less is an open question, but it is one that the present arrangement prevents us from answering.

options.C: people came to value income above leisure once competition for status made relative position matter most.
options.D: governments stopped legislating shorter weeks after the middle of the century, leaving the matter to employers.

passage: Marketers like to say that the strongest brands have communities rather than customers. They point to the owners of a particular make of motorcycle who ride together on weekends and have its emblem tattooed on their arms, to the users of a computer maker's products who queue overnight for a new model and argue online with the users of its rivals, and to the enthusiasts who restore and exhibit a discontinued car long after its manufacturer has stopped caring about it. Some commentators go further and call such groups tribes, or even congregations, complete with rituals, myths and heretics, as though buying a product were the first step in a conversion.

The comparison is not empty. Members of these groups share a body of lore, the founding story, the legendary models, the right and wrong ways to use the product, and newcomers learn it much as initiates learn a tradition. They define themselves partly against outsiders, often the owners of a rival brand, and they police their own boundaries, distinguishing the real enthusiast from the person who has merely bought the thing. Most strikingly, they develop a sense of ownership over the brand that is not legal but moral. When a company alters a celebrated design or moves production to another country, its most loyal customers frequently respond not as disappointed consumers but as betrayed members, as though something that belonged to them had been taken without their consent.

Yet the tribal analogy conceals as much as it reveals. Membership of a tribe is not usually something one buys, and leaving it is not usually as easy as buying something else. A brand community, by contrast, is entered through a purchase and can be abandoned at the price of another. More important, the symbols around which it gathers are the legal property of a firm whose interests are not the members' interests. The firm can redesign the emblem, discontinue the product or sell the brand to a competitor, and the members, however devoted, have no formal say in any of it. A tribe whose totem could be sold at auction would be a strange tribe indeed.

It is tempting to resolve the tension by declaring one side the truth: either the community is an illusion manufactured by advertising, or the commercial setting is incidental and the solidarity is all that matters. Neither will do. The solidarity is real; people form friendships, give one another practical help and find meaning in these groups, and much of this happens without the company's involvement or even against its wishes. But the solidarity is organised around something its members do not control, and that fact shapes it. The anger that follows an unpopular redesign is the anger of people discovering, often for the first time, the limits of an ownership they had felt but never possessed.

A brand community, then, is best understood neither as a tribe that happens to shop nor as a market that happens to feel warm, but as a peculiar hybrid: a genuine collective built on borrowed ground. Firms that grasp this tend to treat their communities with caution, consulting them, deferring to them on matters of heritage and sometimes ceding them real influence over decisions. Firms that do not, and that treat the community merely as a marketing asset to be managed, are apt to learn how quickly devotion can turn into grievance, and how little the language of community protects a firm once its members conclude that they have been treated as an audience rather than as partners.

passage: Spoken irony rarely needs announcing. A slight drag on a word, a flattened pitch, a pause before the punchline: listeners pick up such cues without noticing that they have done so, and the speaker relies on them without noticing either. Writing, however expressive in other respects, strips most of them away. For centuries this mattered less than it might have, because the written forms people used for personal exchange, letters above all, were slow, composed and long enough to establish their own tone over several paragraphs. A letter writer who wished to be ironic had room to prepare the reader for it.

The short typed message removes that room while keeping the pace of speech. Exchanges happen in seconds, between people who often know each other well enough to joke, in fragments too brief to carry their own context. The result is a familiar variety of communicative accident. A remark meant as affectionate teasing arrives as a rebuke; a dry agreement reads as sincere enthusiasm, or the reverse. The writer, who heard the intended tone in his own head as he typed, is often the last to see that it was not on the screen.

Writers have not, however, accepted this deprivation quietly. Over the past few decades they have built, without any committee to guide them, a supplementary system of signals: the small faces and symbols that can be appended to a sentence, the strategic use of capitals and repeated letters, even the presence or absence of a full stop, which among some groups of writers has come to make a short reply sound curt. It is common to lament these devices as a decline in the standards of written language. That complaint misses what they are for. They are not a lazy substitute for vocabulary but a written prosody, an attempt to restore precisely the cues that typing removed.

Yet the new system has a weakness that spoken prosody largely lacks. The meaning of a rising tone is shared across most speakers of a language; the meaning of a particular symbol or a missing full stop is settled within smaller circles and changes quickly. A face that one group uses to soften a criticism may strike another as mocking, and a message read across a gap of age or community can misfire precisely because the writer took care to mark its tone. The invention of written prosody, in other words, has not abolished misreading so much as relocated it, from the gap between voice and text to the gap between the conventions of different readers.

passage: Imagine a small-town bank that is entirely sound: its loans are prudent and its borrowers will repay, although those loans run for years while its deposits can be withdrawn on any day. Suppose a rumour spreads that this institution is in trouble. Each depositor now faces a simple calculation: if others withdraw and I do not, my bank may have to sell its loans in a hurry and at a loss, leaving me with little, whereas if I withdraw first, I lose nothing. It is therefore rational to run whether or not the rumour is true, and once enough people run, the rumour becomes true. Such a bank fails not because it was unsound but because it was believed to be.

Deposit insurance is the classic answer, because a guarantee from the state, up to some limit, alters the calculation entirely. A depositor who stays put loses nothing even if her bank collapses, so she has no reason to join a run, and because no one runs, the guarantee is seldom called upon. Seen in this light, insurance looks almost like a free lunch: a promise that, by being believed, makes its own fulfilment unnecessary.

The objection is familiar. Insured depositors have no reason to ask what their bank does with their money, and a bank whose depositors do not ask can take risks that it would otherwise have to justify to them. The guarantee that ends panics may thus encourage the very recklessness that makes failures likely. Critics conclude that deposit insurance trades a visible problem for a hidden one, and some would scale it back so that depositors once again have a reason to pay attention.

The objection is sound as far as it goes, but it rests on a curious picture of who disciplined banks before guarantees existed. Ordinary depositors were never skilled readers of loan books; what they were skilled at was panic. The discipline they supplied was indiscriminate, falling on sound and unsound banks alike once fear took hold, as the town bank illustrates. If insured depositors stop watching, little genuine scrutiny is lost, and the task passes to those equipped for it: supervisors with the power to inspect, and the large uninsured creditors whose money remains at stake. The lesson of the objection is not that guarantees are a mistake but that they must be paired with oversight, and that the limit on cover matters a great deal, since it decides who still has a reason to care.

passage: Debates about privacy in the age of large data sets usually begin from an image of ownership. Each person, on this view, holds a store of information about themselves, and the moral question is whether that information is taken with or without their permission. Hence the enormous weight placed on consent: the checkbox, the privacy notice, the setting that lets a user decline to share. If people are told what will happen to their data and agree to it, the transaction is treated as legitimate, and if they refuse, they are thought to have protected themselves.

The difficulty is that much personal information is not individual in the way the image assumes. A person who uploads their contact list discloses the names and numbers of people who agreed to nothing. Someone who submits a sample to a genetic testing service reveals facts about parents, siblings and cousins, some of whom may not know the test was taken. More subtly, when enough people share information about their habits, a system can learn the patterns that link one trait to another, and then infer those traits in people who shared nothing at all. A person who declines to disclose, say, a health condition may find that it has been estimated, with fair accuracy, from purchases and movements that resemble those of people who did disclose it.

One might reply that the refuser has still kept their own data, and that what others choose to reveal is their own affair. But this misses what the refuser was trying to protect. Nobody declines to share a fact for the sake of a particular row in a database; they decline because they do not want the fact known. If it can be known anyway, through the choices of others, then the refusal has secured very little, and the consent framework, which places the whole burden of protection on individual decisions, has quietly ceased to describe what is actually happening.

This does not make individual consent worthless. Being asked still matters, and a person who is deceived about how their information will be used has been wronged in a way that the collective character of data does not erase. The point is that consent cannot carry the load it has been given. Privacy behaves in part like clean air or quiet streets: a condition that each person's conduct affects for others, and that no one can secure for themselves by private choice alone. Protecting it therefore requires rules about what may be inferred and done, not merely about who has clicked agree.

passage: Many societies have set aside days on which the ordinary order is turned upside down. In the Roman Saturnalia, masters are said to have waited on their slaves at table; in parts of medieval Europe, junior clergy elected a mock bishop and parodied the liturgy; in countless village festivals men dress as women, children give orders to adults, and the powerful are mocked in songs that would be punished at any other time of year. Such festivals of inversion have long puzzled those who study them, because they seem to put the most fundamental arrangements of a society at risk for the sake of a few days of licence.

Two explanations have dominated. The first, often called the safety valve theory, holds that inversion protects the order it mocks. Resentments that accumulate under hierarchy are released in a bounded, harmless form, and when the festival ends everyone returns to their place, relieved and more willing to stay there. The second reverses the judgement. On this view, the festival gives people a glimpse of a world arranged otherwise, keeps alive the memory that rank is not natural, and so contains the seed of real defiance. Supporters of each view can point to cases. Rulers have tolerated and even funded such festivals, which suggests they found them useful; they have also banned them, which suggests they found them dangerous, and on a few occasions a carnival has indeed turned into a riot.

What both explanations share is the assumption that the meaning of inversion is fixed by its form, so that one need only decide, once and for all, whether turning the world upside down conserves it or threatens it. The historical record does not support so tidy a choice, since the same festival, with the same masks and the same songs, has been a harmless frolic in one decade and the occasion of an uprising in the next. The difference lay not in the ritual but in its circumstances: a bad harvest, a disputed tax, a quarrel between factions of the elite that made the mockery of one of them useful to the other. Inversion, in other words, does not carry its own political charge; it takes one from the situation into which it is performed.

The safety valve theory has a further weakness that is easy to overlook because its central image is so vivid. It pictures discontent as a kind of pressure that builds up in a closed vessel and can be let off in measured bursts. There is little reason to think that resentment, which is attached to particular injuries and particular persons, behaves like steam that can be vented without residue; people who have mocked their masters for a day do not obviously feel less aggrieved afterwards, and they may feel more entitled to their grievance for having heard it voiced aloud by a crowd. The image persuades because it is mechanical, not because anyone has observed the mechanism.

A more promising account starts from a simpler observation. To turn a world upside down, one must first show which way up it is. The mock bishop presupposes a real one; the servant who gives orders for a day makes plain who gives them on every other day. Inversion is thus a vivid lesson in hierarchy, and in that sense it does teach the order it reverses. But the lesson cuts both ways, since a ranking that can be so easily reversed in play is shown to be a convention rather than a fact of nature. Which of these lessons is learned depends, again, on what else is happening. That is an unsatisfying conclusion only for those who wanted the festival to have a single meaning.
